pm-master.title: The master checklist
pm-master.storageNote: Progress saves in this browser as you check items.

items.t: Walk the center: storefronts, sidewalks, parking field, lighting
items.n: Look for trip hazards, burned-out poles, cart damage, standing water.

items.t: Check the main field and remote lots for litter, illegal dumping, and cart corrals
items.n: Remote lots get skipped first; make them an explicit stop.

items.t: Inspect dumpster and rear service areas; confirm gates and enclosure
items.n: Rear-of-house condition shows up in tenant satisfaction first.

items.t: Review tenant communication queue; respond within one business day
items.n: Under the Operator Landlord approach, responsiveness is the product.

items.t: Confirm signage is lit and pylon faces are intact
items.n: Signage is common-area work that directly feeds leasing.

items.t: Run the rent cycle: statements, reminders, escalate delinquencies per the lease
items.n: Courtesy reminder before the first; defined escalation after.

items.t: Reconcile the rent roll to the bank; investigate every variance
items.n: A rent roll that does not match the bank is fiction.

items.t: Review the P&L against budget; annotate significant variances
items.n: An unexplained variance grows. A named explanation can be managed.

items.t: Issue owner report: income, expenses, occupancy, work, decisions needed
items.n: Same format every month — the report is a rhythm, not an event.

items.t: Check certificate of insurance expirations — tenants and vendors
items.n: Request renewals 30 days before lapse, in writing.

items.t: Review aged work orders; nothing open past 30 days without a reason
items.n: Every open order needs an owner and a next step.

items.t: Pull and re-file current COIs for every tenant and active vendor
items.n: Match against the lease-required coverages, not just presence.

items.t: Fire & life-safety inspection: extinguishers, exits, alarms, panels
items.n: Document with dated photos; file in the owner safe.

items.t: Meet or call each key vendor: roof, HVAC, landscaping, paving, security
items.n: Ask what they are seeing that you are not.

items.t: Review the critical-dates board: expirations, options, notice windows
items.n: Anything inside 12 months gets a named next step.

items.t: Walk the roof (or schedule the walk) and inspect fascia, gutters, drains
items.n: Roof problems are cheap at quarterly cadence and expensive at annual.

items.t: Test site lighting photometrics at night; replace dark poles
items.n: Lighting drives both safety perception and evening sales.

items.t: Spring: full exterior refresh — landscaping, pressure washing, striping touch-up
items.n: Curb appeal is leasing inventory.

items.t: Pre-summer (Gulf South by June 1): storm prep — trees trimmed, drains cleared, loose items secured
items.n: Document pre-storm condition with dated photos.

items.t: Summer: HVAC service verified on every suite; confirm contract coverage
items.n: Summer HVAC failure is a tenant-relations event, not a maintenance item.

items.t: Fall: parking lot inspection — cracks sealed before freeze or wet season
items.n: Water enters cracks; what freezes or floods lifts asphalt.

items.t: Winter: holiday operations plan — parking, signage, extended hours lighting
items.n: Set it in October, not November.

items.t: Build the operating budget for next year; set the reserve contribution
items.n: Fund the roofs and lots you already know you own.

items.t: Complete CAM reconciliation against actuals per the lease deadlines
items.n: Deadlines are lease obligations — verify your own language.

items.t: Full property condition survey: roof, envelope, paving, site, signage
items.n: Feed findings into the capital plan and the reserve study.

items.t: Insurance renewal review: values, coverages, claims history, bids
items.n: Start 120 days before expiry; never renew on autopilot.

items.t: Property tax assessment review; file appeals where warranted
items.n: Deadlines are jurisdictional — calendar them at the start of the year.

items.t: Update the emergency and continuity plan; confirm contact tree
items.n: Include tenants, vendors, insurer, counsel, and utilities.

items.t: A one-to-two-page abstract for every tenant, verified against the executed lease
items.n: Dates, rent schedule, options, exclusives, CAM treatment, notices.

items.t: Every executed lease, amendment, and side letter filed and named consistently
items.n: Suite_Tenant_DocumentType_Date.

items.t: Security deposit and guaranty on record for every suite
items.n: Note the gaps; missing deposits surface at the worst times.

items.t: Renewal alert set at 12 / 9 / 6 months before every expiration
items.n: Late renewal conversations are negotiated from weakness.

items.t: A vendor table: scope, contract terms, rates, COI expiration, contacts
items.n: One table, one home, current to the month.

items.t: Every service contract reviewed before auto-renewal
items.n: Diarize renewal windows the day the contract is signed.

items.t: Warranties on capital work filed in the owner safe with expiration dates
items.n: A warranty you cannot find is a warranty you do not have.

items.t: One source of truth for leases, vendors, work orders, and financials
items.n: If it is not in the system, it did not happen.

items.t: Backup verified: exports run, restore tested, off-site copy current
items.n: A backup that has never been restored is a hope.

items.t: Access review: who can reach the records, banking, and accounts — and should they
items.n: Quarterly, and after any staffing change.

items.t: The checklist itself reviewed and revised
items.n: Add what was missed; remove what no longer serves the property.

doc-safe.title: The owner document safe
doc-safe.storageNote: Progress saves in this browser as you check items.

items.t: Formation documents and operating agreement for every owning entity
items.n: Including amendments — the version history matters.

items.t: EIN records and registered agent documentation
items.n: Required for banking, tax filings, and counsel.

items.t: Recorded warranty deeds and the complete chain of title instruments
items.n: The paper that proves the asset is yours.

items.t: Title insurance policy and closing documents from acquisition
items.n: The title policy is the first call when a boundary or servitude question arises.

items.t: Corporate resolutions or authorizations naming who may act for the entity
items.n: Banks and title companies will ask for these.

items.t: The recorded plat and all recorded revisions
items.n: For a legacy center, the plat is the operating map — parking, easements, setbacks.

items.t: Surveys: original, ALTA/NSPS, and any as-builts
items.n: Marked-up survey copies belong here too.

items.t: Zoning records: classification, variances, and conditions of approval
items.n: Legacy variances (parking, green area) are assets — keep the paper that proves them.

items.t: Environmental reports: Phase I, Phase II, and any remediation records
items.n: Lenders and buyers will request these in every transaction.

items.t: Easements and servitudes: reciprocal access, utility, signage
items.n: Include recorded exhibits and a simple indexed list.

items.t: Every executed lease, amendment, side letter, and exhibit — complete and ordered
items.n: Sequence matters: a missing amendment changes what the lease says.

items.t: A verified lease abstract for every suite
items.n: One to two pages; verified against the executed documents.

items.t: Estoppel certificates collected from tenants at acquisition and refinance
items.n: Filed by suite, with the date of the certifying statement.

items.t: Guaranties and personal undertakings
items.n: Note which are active and which have been released.

items.t: Insurance obligations per lease: required coverages and minimum limits
items.n: So COIs can be checked against something written.

items.t: All property policies, renewals, and endorsements — current and historical
items.n: Historical policies matter for claims with long tails.

items.t: Claims file: FNOL, adjuster correspondence, settlements, and reserves
items.n: Close every claim to a final paper trail.

items.t: Tenant and vendor COIs, current year plus recent history
items.n: The active expirations also live in the operating system.

items.t: Flood and wind documentation where applicable — maps, elevation certificates, policies
items.n: In Gulf South markets, this family is first-class, not an afterthought.

items.t: Loan documents: note, mortgage, guarantees, and every amendment or modification
items.n: Include lender-required reporting commitments.

items.t: Appraisals and inspection reports from acquisition and refinance
items.n: They benchmark value in future conversations.

items.t: Tax assessments, bills, and appeal records by year
items.n: Win an appeal once and the record pays for itself annually.

items.t: Year-end financial statements and depreciation schedules
items.n: Hand your accountant a complete year, not an archaeology project.

items.t: Major service contracts: roof, HVAC, paving, landscaping, security
items.n: Diarized with expiration and renewal windows.

items.t: Capital work records: contracts, warranties, permits, and completion documents
items.n: Warranty + proof of install = enforceable protection.

items.t: Utilities: account numbers, meter locations, and service contracts
items.n: Someone other than you should be able to transfer service in an emergency.

items.t: The one-page access map: where the safe is, how it is organized, who holds keys and passwords
items.n: Sealed with counsel or a partner — the safe must survive its owner.

items.t: Redundancy verified: three copies, two media, one off-site — tested this year
items.n: A copy that has never been opened is a rumor.

items.t: Confirm property type: open-air, strip, neighborhood, power, lifestyle
Verify GLA and anchor/inline split

Confirm occupancy rate (physical vs. economic)

Check co-tenancy clause exposure
Review trailing 12-month (T12) operating statement
Identify deferred maintenance from broker tour
Confirm parking ratio (minimum 4.0/1,000 sf)
Check zoning and permitted uses

Add back owner-managed expenses to market rate
Verify CAM recovery ratio (target: 85–95%)
Model vacancy at 5–10% stabilized
Calculate management fee at 3–5% EGI
Confirm CapEx reserve: $0.50–$1.50/sf/yr
Stress-test DSCR at 1.25x minimum
Model anchor vacancy scenario
Confirm debt coverage at market rate financing
Build 5-year hold model with exit cap
Abstract all leases: base rent, term, options, CAM, exclusives
Flag co-tenancy clauses and trigger conditions
Identify exclusivity restrictions on future leasing
Confirm personal guaranty on all leases
Review percentage rent clauses and breakpoints
Check ROFO/ROFR provisions
Identify lease termination rights
Confirm assignment and subletting restrictions
Review holdover rent provisions
Flag any below-market leases with long remaining terms
Commission Phase I Environmental Site Assessment
Review Phase I — flag RECs for Phase II
Inspect roof: age, condition, warranty status
Inspect HVAC: age, tonnage, maintenance history
Review parking lot: condition, ADA compliance, lighting
Inspect electrical panels and service capacity
Review plumbing and fire suppression systems
Confirm ADA compliance: accessible routes, restrooms
Review signage: pylon, building, monument
Obtain contractor bids for deferred maintenance items
Order ALTA/NSPS survey
Review REAs, easements, and CC and Rs
Confirm parking easements and shared access
Identify encroachments or boundary issues
Review title commitment — flag Schedule B exceptions
Confirm no mechanics' liens
Verify flood zone status (FEMA)
Review reciprocal easement agreements with anchors
Confirm utility easements and access
Order title insurance: owner's and lender's policies
Pull prior-year CAM budget vs. actual comparison
Categorize all expenses: includable vs. excludable
Remove capital expenditures from CAM pool
Remove management fee if excluded by lease
Remove anchor-specific expenses if excluded
Apply gross-up calculation for vacant spaces
Calculate each tenant's pro-rata share
Apply controllable CAM cap (typically 3–5%)
Prepare reconciliation statement per tenant
Send statements within 90–120 days of year-end
Capital improvements (roof replacement, parking lot reseal)
Depreciation on capital items
Leasing commissions and tenant improvement costs
Marketing fund contributions (if separate)
Anchor tenant spaces (if excluded by REA)
Costs covered by insurance proceeds
Management fee (if lease excludes)
Legal fees for lease disputes
Income taxes on landlord entity
Financing costs and debt service
Maintain all vendor invoices for 3 years
Keep CAM ledger reconciled monthly
Document gross-up methodology in writing
Confirm audit rights window (typically 12–24 months)
Prepare summary of includable expense categories
Document all exclusions applied with lease citations
Maintain allocation methodology for shared costs
Keep copies of all reconciliation statements sent
Confirm default: missed payment, partial payment, or NSF
Check lease for notice requirements and cure period
Send formal written demand via certified mail
Document date of default and amount owed
Calculate late fees per lease terms
Review acceleration clause — decide whether to invoke
Assess tenant's financial condition and history
Determine: accept cure, negotiate, or proceed to eviction
If the cure period has ended: stop. Hand the notice, the ledger, and the lease to counsel before any possession filing
Do not change locks, shut off utilities, or exclude the occupant yourself. Self-help is not an operator step
Document the specific default (unauthorized use, sublease, etc.)
Review lease for cure period (typically 30 days)
Send written notice of default with specific cure requirement
Photograph or document the default condition
Set calendar reminder for cure period expiration
Assess whether default is curable or incurable
If the default may be incurable: ask counsel whether the lease allows termination, and wait for that answer
Document all communications with tenant
Secure premises immediately after possession
Change locks and alarm codes
Conduct condition assessment and photograph everything
Prepare cost estimate for restoration to leasable condition
Pursue guarantor if personal guaranty exists
File claim for unpaid rent, damages, and re-leasing costs
Engage broker for re-leasing within 30 days
Update rent roll and financial model for vacancy
Obtain W-9 and verify entity type
Collect certificate of insurance (COI)
Verify minimum coverage: $1M GL, $2M aggregate, $1M auto
Confirm landlord named as additional insured
Execute written service agreement before work begins
Define scope of work, pricing, and payment terms
Establish performance standards and KPIs
Confirm licensing and bonding requirements
Verify workers' compensation coverage
Set up vendor in accounting system
Track COI expiration dates (calendar reminders 60 days out)
Conduct quarterly performance reviews for major vendors
Document complaints and service failures in writing
Compare invoices to contract pricing monthly
Conduct annual competitive bid for contracts over $10K/yr
Review landscaping: frequency, quality, seasonal schedule
Review HVAC: PM schedule, response time, parts markup
Review janitorial: frequency, scope, supply costs
Review security: coverage hours, incident reporting
Review parking lot: sweeping, striping, lighting maintenance
Review contract for termination notice requirements
Send written termination notice per contract terms
Secure all property access (keys, codes, badges)
Obtain final invoice and reconcile open balances
Document reason for termination in vendor file
Transition work to replacement vendor before termination effective date
Retain all documentation for 3 years

res-pct.title: Percentage Rent Audit Worksheet
res-pct.storageNote: Progress saves in this browser. The printable blank is the download on the Resources shelf.

items.t: All cash and credit card sales from the leased premises
Online orders fulfilled from or picked up at the premises (if lease covers omnichannel)
Gift card redemptions (at time of redemption, not issuance)
Layaway payments (at time of completion)
Delivery charges billed to customers
Sales by sublicensees or concessionaires operating within the space

sections.title: Standard Exclusions (confirm these are NOT counted)

items.t: Sales tax collected and remitted to government
Returns and allowances (net of restocking fees)
Employee discounts (up to lease cap, typically 5–10% of sales)
Gift card issuances (not redemptions)
Transfers between tenant locations (inter-store transfers)
Sales of fixtures, equipment, or assets not in ordinary course
Insurance proceeds
Bad debt write-offs (if lease permits)

res-skill.title: Shopping Center PM Skill Matrix
res-skill.storageNote: Progress saves in this browser. The printable blank is the download on the Resources shelf.

items.t: Score every row at a whole level from 1 to 5
items.n: A level 4 still includes the work at level 2.

items.t: Circle the two rows with the widest gap between where you are and where the center needs you
items.n: Those two are the quarter.

items.t: Name one artifact for each circled row
items.n: A reconciliation, a renewal memo, a capital plan, or a report. Reading is not the artifact.

items.t: Put a 90-day rescore on the calendar
items.n: Score the artifact, not the intention.

sections.title: Before this blank leaves the office

items.t: Company legal name is the entity that will originate the debit
A prior owner's name, logo, or account is not on the page
Amounts and dates live in the lease or a schedule, and the form points at that writing
The revocation contact is a real address or inbox
Counsel and the bank or processor have reviewed this wording for your originator agreement
The signed original is filed with the lease, and the copy you keep does not become the next tenant's form

items.t: Takeover: sections 2 and 3 inside 30 days of appointment
Ordinary weeks: section 5 (calendar), section 6 (priorities), section 11 (walk)
Money: section 8 and section 9 at the quarterly owner review, and again at the annual plan
A loss or an after-hours failure: section 10 first, then the vendor list in section 7

sections.title: Thirty days before, or as soon as you have access

items.t: Prior work-order history exported, including anything still open
Vendor list with contract end dates and certificate end dates
Roof, HVAC, fire, and lot warranties located, not described from memory
As-built drawings compared with one walk. Note every mismatch
Keys, codes, and alarm accounts inventoried. Plan the change for day one
Open capital jobs named, with who pays and who is on site
After-hours roster confirmed: HVAC, electrical, plumbing, roof, board-up, glass
Utility account numbers and meter locations written down
Known leaks, trip hazards, and dark poles listed with a photo
Tenant contacts for facilities, not only for rent

sections.title: Seven days before, and day one

items.t: Alarm and after-hours test placed on the calendar
Vendors told, in writing, who may approve work and who may not
First walk scheduled with the outgoing manager, every service yard included
Photo set of each elevation, the lot, and the roof access stored with the date
Every row has a name in the last column, or an explicit "none this month"
Each filled cell names a vendor or an in-house owner
Statutory tests (alarm, sprinkler, backflow, hood) show the certificate, not only the visit
Every order has one owner. "The team" is not an owner
Closure includes a photo or a note of what "done" means
Anything open past your own limit has a written reason
W-9 and entity name match the contract
Certificate of insurance on file, landlord as additional insured where you require it
License checked where the trade requires one
Workers' compensation on file where the law requires it
Scope, price, and who may approve extras are in a writing signed before work
Certificate end date is on a calendar 30 days ahead, and access stops when the certificate lapses
Major contracts (janitorial, landscape, HVAC service, sweeping) have a rebid or a written reason not to rebid on a cycle you chose
Invoices are compared with the contract rate before they are paid
A five-year list exists, even if years three through five are ranges
Reserves are a number someone can find, not a percentage mentioned once
Water, power, and gas shutoffs are located and labeled
Tenants have a written way to reach you after hours
After a P1, a short note of what happened and what changed is filed within seven days
Storefront glass, walks, and the accessible route
Lot: litter, dumping, carts, striping, lights out
Service yards, enclosures, and gates
Pylon and monument faces, including faces that should be dark because the suite is dark
Standing water, and inlets that did not clear the last rain
Anything a customer would photograph. Write it down before they do
A tenant work request is logged even when the lease makes it the tenant's repair
After-hours work that closes an entrance is noticed ahead of time, with a named contact

sections.title: 15. Retail conditions worth a line of their own

items.t: Food tenants: hood, exhaust, and grease interceptor on a schedule, with the last service date
Sign criteria exist, and a new face is checked against them before it is built
Anchor or major-tenant facilities contact is a person you have met
Tenant build-out: penetrations, exhaust, and sprinklers are reviewed before work, and the drawing on file matches what was built
Shared access or drainage that crosses a property line is in the file, not only in someone's head

items.t: Where does the rent roll disagree with the executed leases?
Which dates in the next 24 months change rent, an option, or a termination right?
What is vacant, what is dark, and what is only occupied on the roll?
Which categories would a shopper expect here, and which are missing?
What did the center recover last year, and which leases block a recovery?
What is the condition of roof, HVAC, lot, and life safety, and who pays for each?
Which vendors are on site, and which certificates lapse inside 90 days?
What does ownership receive every month, and who writes it?
Where does the lease put a repair, and where has practice drifted?
What would strain a loan covenant or an insurance condition this quarter?
What is the after-hours path, and when did someone last walk it?
